cards.fact: Trembling aspen regrows after fire or cutting mainly from root suckers, so a whole aspen stand is often one genetic clone that leafs out and turns gold together.
cards.source: Perala 1990, Populus tremuloides, in Silvics of North America vol. 2 (USDA Agric. Handb. 654)

cards.fact: Balsam fir is shade tolerant: its seedlings wait for decades in the understorey and take over the canopy gaps left as old aspen and spruce die, a classic late-succession step in Ontario's boreal forest.
cards.source: Frank 1990, Abies balsamea, in Silvics of North America vol. 1 (USDA Agric. Handb. 654)

cards.fact: Paper birch bark is rich in betulin, a white waxy compound that makes it waterproof and rot resistant; it was used for canoes, containers and roofing across the boreal forest.
cards.source: Safford, Bjorkbom & Zasada 1990, Betula papyrifera, in Silvics of North America vol. 2

cards.fact: Lake of the Woods, at Kenora, has more than 14,500 islands and about 105,000 km of shoreline; it drains north through the Winnipeg River to Hudson Bay.
cards.source: Lake of the Woods Water Sustainability Foundation, State of the Basin Report (2014)

cards.fact: Beaver dams turn streams into ponds that drown the trees behind them; when a pond is abandoned and the dam breaks, it drains into a sedge 'beaver meadow' that can last for decades.
Jack pine cones are sealed with resin that melts at about 50 °C, so a fire opens them and reseeds the burn. That is why jack pine dominates dry, sandy and rocky Shield sites that burn often.
cards.source: Rudolph & Laidly 1990, Pinus banksiana, in Silvics of North America vol. 1

cards.fact: In summer, moose wade into ponds to eat aquatic plants, which are richer in sodium than land browse; this helps them meet a mineral need that woody twigs cannot.
Snowshoe hares in the boreal forest rise and crash on a cycle of about ten years, and lynx numbers follow one to two years behind.
